reason: Facts show a recent CHF stay and documented transfer/ADL deficits, so restorative therapy is plausibly skilled, but routine self-care and strength work may be nonskilled and daily skilled need is not established.

A 13-day hospital stay supports the three-day requirement, and repeated medication adjustments suggest some skilled observation, but inpatient status and direct admission are not shown, so coverage is at most partial.

The services were inpatient ICD replacements with short expected stays that the QIO said could be denied inpatient billing; the appellant contests only liability, which does not make the admissions covered.
The facts are purely procedural and show no qualifying stay, skilled need or covered service, so coverage is not supported.
Admission followed a qualifying stay with skilled PT until the plateau on February 7, supporting early coverage, while later days lack a skilled need.
Home health at an assisted living facility can be covered if reasonable and necessary, but homebound status, skilled need and duplication of facility services are not shown.
All billed dates fall after both therapies were discharged, and no skilled service on those dates appears in the facts.
Nursing observation and insulin adjustments support skilled care, but observation is covered only until stabilization and she tested her own sugar, so only part is supported.
A qualifying stay and timely admission are shown and skilled monitoring is documented around March 2-6, but daily skilled need is shown only for about a week.
Admission followed a qualifying stay and therapy continued to September 30, supporting that period, but readmission evaluation and later dates are not shown.
A new decline after the fall supports a brief period of skilled PT, but goals were met by September 11 and general exercise is not skilled.
Stair-lift transfer teaching and maintenance program design by a therapist can be skilled, but visits solely to train aides and aide visits are not supported.
Infections, abscesses and a fistula support some skilled nursing visits, but routine ostomy care is not skilled and visit-level documentation is lacking.
Part-time or intermittent aide and nursing care is covered only within the 28 to 35 hour weekly limits and only if reasonable and necessary.
The beneficiary was placed in a noncertified bed, which is generally not covered, and payment depends on an unestablished limitation of liability.
The facts contain no clinical information showing the IRF requirements were met, so coverage is not supported.
Skilled monitoring, pneumonia care and PT support coverage early in the period, but behavior stabilized by August 12 so late August is doubtful.
Ongoing IV/IM medication and severe pain suggest she was still completing hospital treatment and could not yet take part in intensive rehabilitation, and the IRF requirements are not shown.
